name: Hobbyamory
summary: A New York Times-coined term (August 2026) for young singles who fill their calendars with hobbies, clubs and friends instead of dating, now spreading through newsletters and international press.
what: Hobbyamory describes singles putting their time and money into a range of hobbies and friendships rather than dating apps or hookups. Run clubs, pottery, trivia, mahjong and book clubs become their social life, and dating can happen there but is not the goal. It links dating-app fatigue, the Gen Z hobby revival and the 'solo-maxxing' single-by-choice framing.

origin.text: YPulse (2026-08-12) credits the New York Times with coining 'hobbyamory'. The original NYT article did not surface in search; a Dayton Daily News print edition carried what appears to be a syndicated version.

adopters.text: Gen Z and young millennial singles, especially those tired of dating apps, who join hobby classes, clubs and events. Eventbrite data reported by industry press shows hobby events tagged for meeting people growing sharply.

spread.text: Picked up within days in Italy (Il Foglio), by YPulse twice, a women's health outlet, a culture newsletter and US regional print. That is about 4–5 independent signals over 7 weeks. It has not yet been found on TikTok as a hashtag.

trajectory.text: A newly coined term (August 2026) with a handful of independent pickups and no product supply found. The underlying behavior (hobby events instead of apps) has reported data behind it, but the term's consumer use is unproven.

productDemand.text: No purchase evidence for hobbyamory products. Reported growth in hobby events for singles shows people spend time and money on the behavior, and analog planners sell well with Gen Z in general. Purchase intent for a themed planner is unproven.

competition.text: No hobbyamory-named products surfaced. Single-life self-care journals and generic hobby planners exist, but direct marketplace checks were not possible.

gap.text: A 2027 planner built around monthly hobby 'side quests', invitations and friendship tracking for happily single people. It is not a self-care journal and not a dating planner.

window.estimate: Nov 2026 – Feb 2027 (New Year planning plus Valentine's-season single content)
window.reasoning: Planner buying peaks around New Year, and Valentine's season brings single-life content in early February. The behavior is durable even if the term fades.
invalidators: The term gets no new pickups after August
Coverage frames it as a fad and consumers do not adopt the word
window.seasonality: New Year planning; Valentine's / Galentine's in February

rights.note: Do not reference the New York Times. Check the coined term for trademarks before using it in titles. No venue or app names.

timing.rationale: The term is about 7 weeks old and the New Year planning window is ahead.

buyerIntent.rationale: Behavior spend is reported (events), but there is no product purchase evidence.

supplyGap.rationale: No themed products found; marketplaces not checked directly.

productFit.rationale: Translates into a social or hobby planner, but the term itself may not be what buyers search for.

durability.rationale: Dating-app fatigue and the hobby revival are durable; the term is uncertain.

economics.rationale: A digital product with zero marginal cost.

actionRationale: It is a first spark with clear behavior data and no supply. Build the planner cheaply under generic search terms ('2027 planner', 'single life planner') and use 'hobbyamory' only as a hook if it spreads.

products.buyer: US single adults aged 22–35 with dating-app fatigue who are filling their lives with hobbies, clubs and friends
products.theme: 'Side Quest Season 2027': a planner for the happily single and hobby-full, with monthly side quests and a friendship tracker
products.whyBuy: The press says young singles are swapping dates for hobbies ('hobbyamory'), and hobby events for meeting people are reported up sharply. New Year planning is when they will map out 2027's classes and clubs.
products.differentiation: Combines monthly side quests, invitations and friendship tracking; existing single-life products are self-care journals and hobby planners track projects.
products.validationTest: List by Oct 25; 10 pins and 3 videos over 14 days.
products.continueIf: At least 1 sale or 20+ favorites in 21 days, or a side-quest pin passing 100 saves.
products.pivotIf: Interest in the idea lists but no sales: sell the 100-side-quest deck alone at $4, or reposition as a general 'social planner 2027'.
products.stopIf: Under 50 visits after 21 days of promotion.
products.rightsNote: Do not use the New York Times name. Check 'hobbyamory' on USPTO TESS before using it in titles; keep it out of the product pages.

unresolved: Confirm spread: a #hobbyamory hashtag appearing on TikTok or Instagram, or US lifestyle outlets (beyond syndication) using the term in October–November.
Check whether the term appears in end-of-year 'words of 2026' or dating-trend lists in December.
Verify the Eventbrite figures in the original release.
